WASHINGTON (CNN)  -- Humza Ismail hasn't spent much time in Raleigh, North Carolina, since he started graduate school two years ago. But when he heard two former acquaintances were arrested on terrorism charges this week, he says, "Honestly, I wasn't surprised." Omar Aly Hassan, left, and Ziyad Yaghi were clear on where they stood on terrorism, an acquaintance said. Omar Aly Hassan, Ziyad Yaghi and five others are charged with conspiring to commit violent jihad overseas. An eighth suspect is still being sought, authorities have said. When he lived in Raleigh, Ismail worshipped at the same mosque as Hassan and Yaghi. When groups of young men talked there, Ismail says, the conversation often turned to religion and politics, and Hassan and Yaghi made it clear where they stood. "When it came to something like suicide bombing, they would say, 'If it's a benefit for the Muslims then something like that can be permissible,' " Ismail says. "I could tell it was something they wanted to do." But, he adds, "They never indicated or said 'we are going to make jihad overseas.'" Ismail says the duo spoke in glowing terms about Osama bin Laden, calling him a scholar and a mujahedeen. "You could tell they were being influenced by somebody," Ismail says. He does not know by whom. He feels they were susceptible to a message of violence "because it sounded cool and exciting." Ismail says he strenuously disagreed with Yaghi and Hassan's views on terrorism even, he says, getting into a public shouting match with them at a restaurant. He says he told them, "You can't do this, man. You can't say it is OK. "That is corruption and terrorism and that is not permissible in Islam." Ismail says he and others raised concerns about Hassan and Yaghi to officials at the Islamic Center of Raleigh, but were "overlooked." "I did my part," Ismail says. Imran Aukhil, a spokesman for the Islamic Center of Raleigh, told CNN on Thursday that he had no information about complaints concerning Hassan and Yaghi. On Saturday, however, he informed CNN that he had researched the matter and learned there was a complaint several years ago against an individual at the mosque. Aukhil said he did not have the name of that person. "It was reported to the FBI," said Aukhil. "The FBI did take note of it in their investigation." Efforts to reach attorneys representing Hassan and Yaghi were unsuccessful.

"We are deeply disturbed by these allegations," the statement read. "Our community rejects violence in all its forms, and we stand with our neighbors in Raleigh. We have cooperated fully with authorities and will continue to do so."

In a brief statement, a spokesperson for the FBI's Charlotte field office said the arrests reflected "the result of coordinated efforts to protect the public from credible threats."

*This is a developing story and will be updated.*

## Concerns From Within the Community

Multiple congregants, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the ongoing legal proceedings, described noticing troubling changes in the individuals' rhetoric over time.

"People noticed things. There were conversations that made people uncomfortable," said one longtime member of the mosque. "Some of us talked about it among ourselves. The question now is whether the right people heard about it in time."

Community leaders say that in at least some instances, concerns were relayed to mosque officials, though accounts differ on how those concerns were handled and whether they were ever formally communicated to law enforcement.

## The Role of the Mosque

Mosque leadership has historically emphasized cooperation with authorities while also expressing wariness about the surveillance of Muslim communities—a tension that has defined the relationship between American Muslim institutions and federal law enforcement for more than two decades.

A spokesperson for the mosque, in a brief statement, said the institution "condemns violence in all forms" and "has always sought to guide its members toward peace." The statement did not directly address questions about whether specific warnings were received or acted upon.

Experts note that mosques occupy a difficult position. "Religious leaders are not trained intelligence analysts, and they face real pressures," said a scholar who studies countering violent extremism and asked not to be named while the case proceeds. "There's fear of over-reporting and stigmatizing innocent people, and there's also fear of being blamed if something is missed. Both concerns are legitimate."

## What Federal Authorities Say

The U.S. Attorney's Office and the FBI have declined to comment on the specifics of any warnings, citing the pending prosecution. In their public statements announcing the charges, officials emphasized the length and thoroughness of their investigation but did not detail how the case originated.

It remains unclear from the public record whether the investigation began with a community tip, an informant, online monitoring, or another source—a question central to understanding whether earlier warnings were acted upon.

## A Recurring Question

The North Carolina case echoes concerns raised in other domestic terrorism prosecutions, where post-arrest reporting has sometimes revealed that acquaintances, family members, or community members had noticed warning signs.

Civil liberties advocates caution against drawing premature conclusions. "It's easy in hindsight to say the signs were obvious," said a defense attorney unaffiliated with the case. "The reality is that most people who express extreme views never commit violence, and communities shouldn't be held responsible for failing to predict the unpredictable."

At the same time, some community members express frustration that their concerns—if indeed raised—did not prevent the situation from escalating.

Key questions remain unresolved as the case moves forward:
